questions.stimulusTitle: Why Some Cities Build Rain Gardens
questions.stimulusText:
During a heavy storm, water runs off roofs, sidewalks, parking lots, and streets. In areas covered by many hard surfaces, much of that water cannot soak directly into the ground. It may instead flow rapidly into storm drains, sometimes carrying soil, litter, and other materials with it.
A rain garden is a shallow planted area designed to temporarily collect some of this runoff. It is usually placed where water naturally flows from a roof, driveway, or paved area. The garden's soil and plants slow the water and allow part of it to soak into the ground.
Rain gardens are not simply ordinary flower beds placed in wet locations. Designers consider the amount of runoff, how quickly the soil drains, and which plants can tolerate both wet and dry periods. A garden that holds water too long may not function as intended, while one that drains too quickly may capture little runoff.
A single rain garden cannot solve every storm-water problem in a neighborhood. However, many small features can work together with drains, ponds, and other systems. They can also add vegetation to developed areas.
For planners, the value of a rain garden lies partly in its scale. It is a relatively small feature, but when carefully located and designed, it can help manage water close to where the rain falls.

questions.stimulusText:
An old map can look authoritative. Its lines are precise, its place names are carefully written, and its symbols seem to turn a complicated landscape into an orderly page. Yet historians do not treat a map as a perfectly neutral picture of the world.
Every map reflects choices. A mapmaker decides what area to include, what to leave out, which features deserve labels, and how large or prominent those features should appear. A harbor map may emphasize water depth and channels, while a political map may highlight borders. Neither map is necessarily inaccurate simply because it focuses on different information.
The map's intended audience also matters. A document prepared for merchants may identify roads, ports, and market towns. A military map from the same period may devote more attention to hills, bridges, and defensive positions. Comparing the two can reveal not only geographic information but also the priorities of the people who made and used them.
Historians therefore ask questions beyond “Where was this place?” They ask who produced the map, for whom, and for what purpose. They may compare it with letters, surveys, or later maps.
Seen this way, a map is both a source of geographic evidence and a record of human decisions. Its usefulness increases when readers examine what it shows, what it omits, and why those choices may have been made.

questions.stimulusText:
Mara had agreed to help her neighbor Mr. Ito prepare a courtyard for the evening block gathering. Her job seemed simple: hang a row of paper lanterns beneath the covered walkway. Mr. Ito handed her a wooden box containing lanterns he had used for years.
Mara worked quickly until she noticed that one lantern had a narrow tear near its base. She considered placing it at the far end, where few people would notice. Instead, she carried it to Mr. Ito and apologized, assuming she had damaged it.
He examined the tear and smiled. “That happened last spring,” he said. “I kept it because the frame is still good.”
Together they cut a piece of translucent paper and fitted it behind the torn section. The patch did not disappear. When the lantern was lit, it formed a darker shape across one side.
That evening, Mara watched visitors pass beneath the row. No one complained about the patched lantern. A small child even pointed to it and said the shadow looked like a mountain.
Mara had begun the afternoon thinking that a repaired object was merely a second-best version of a new one. By the time she left, she understood why Mr. Ito had kept the lantern: usefulness did not always require perfection.

questions.stimulusTitle: The Work Behind a Museum Label
questions.stimulusText:
A museum label may contain only a few sentences, but producing those sentences can require substantial research. Before a label is installed beside an object, museum staff must decide which facts are both reliable and useful to visitors.
The process often begins with records about the object's origin, materials, maker, or previous owners. Curators may compare these records with photographs, catalogs, letters, or scientific analysis. Sometimes the evidence is incomplete. In that case, a careful label distinguishes what is known from what is uncertain rather than presenting a guess as fact.
Writers also consider the visitor's experience. A label cannot include everything specialists know. If it becomes overloaded with dates and technical terms, readers may miss the central idea. Staff therefore select details that help explain why the object matters, while additional information may be provided through digital guides or longer publications.
Labels can also change. New research may correct an old identification, clarify an object's history, or provide a better interpretation of its use. Updating a label is not necessarily evidence that earlier staff were careless. It can show that historical knowledge develops as new evidence appears.
The small rectangle beside an exhibit is therefore the visible result of choices about evidence, accuracy, emphasis, and audience.

Pine needles covered the ground, and a fallen branch hid one of the wooden trail markers.

questions.prompt: What happens to wind on the downwind side of a properly designed snow fence?

choices.A: It speeds up sharply.
choices.B: It slows down.
choices.C: It stops completely.

questions.stimulusText:
A snow fence does not stop snow from falling, and it is not designed to catch every flake that blows toward it. Instead, it changes the movement of wind near the ground.
When moving air reaches a properly designed snow fence, some air passes through the openings while some flows over the top. The wind slows on the downwind side. Because slower air can carry less blowing snow, snow particles settle out and form a drift at a predictable distance from the fence.
Placement matters. If a fence is installed too close to a road, the resulting drift may form where snow removal crews least want it. Engineers therefore consider typical wind direction, expected snow volume, fence height, and the distance between the fence and the area being protected.
Snow fences can be made from wooden slats, plastic mesh, or even rows of shrubs. Living rows of vegetation may provide additional benefits, such as wildlife habitat, but they take time to grow and require suitable land.
The key idea is counterintuitive: the fence protects a road or building not by creating a solid wall, but by deliberately causing snow to settle somewhere safer. Its success depends on guiding wind and snow rather than simply blocking them.

questions.stimulusText:
In the early days of detailed city mapping, a finished map could represent months of walking, measuring, comparing records, and redrawing lines. Yet some of the most revealing parts of a mapmaker's work never appeared in the printed map. They remained in field notebooks and margin notes.
A surveyor might record that a lane had recently changed names, that a bridge was being rebuilt, or that residents used a shortcut absent from official records. Such notes helped explain why two sources disagreed. They also reminded the mapmaker which details were uncertain and needed another visit.
Modern researchers sometimes value these working notes for a different reason. A printed map presents decisions as settled: one name is chosen, one boundary is drawn, one road is included. Notes can reveal the questions behind those decisions. They show that maps are constructed from evidence that may be incomplete, changing, or disputed.
This does not make maps unreliable. Rather, it helps readers understand mapping as a process of judgment as well as measurement. A careful mapmaker does not merely collect facts; the mapmaker evaluates sources, notices changes, and decides how best to represent a place at a particular moment.
The margins, then, can preserve something the clean final map cannot: a record of uncertainty being examined rather than hidden.

questions.correctAnswer: Working notes can reveal the judgments and uncertainties behind a finished map.
questions.explanation: The passage focuses on reasoning and uncertainty preserved in mapmakers' notes.
questions.stimulusText:
In the early days of detailed city mapping, a finished map could represent months of walking, measuring, comparing records, and redrawing lines. Yet some of the most revealing parts of a mapmaker's work never appeared in the printed map. They remained in field notebooks and margin notes.
A surveyor might record that a lane had recently changed names, that a bridge was being rebuilt, or that residents used a shortcut absent from official records. Such notes helped explain why two sources disagreed. They also reminded the mapmaker which details were uncertain and needed another visit.
Modern researchers sometimes value these working notes for a different reason. A printed map presents decisions as settled: one name is chosen, one boundary is drawn, one road is included. Notes can reveal the questions behind those decisions. They show that maps are constructed from evidence that may be incomplete, changing, or disputed.
This does not make maps unreliable. Rather, it helps readers understand mapping as a process of judgment as well as measurement. A careful mapmaker does not merely collect facts; the mapmaker evaluates sources, notices changes, and decides how best to represent a place at a particular moment.
The margins, then, can preserve something the clean final map cannot: a record of uncertainty being examined rather than hidden.
